alignment.note: Greek ὁ δέ ('but he') uses an articular substantive with the postpositive connective δέ; the Peshitta replicates this with ܗܘ ܕܝܢ, but the Vulgate compresses the whole into the relative pronoun Qui, subordinating the clause to the preceding narrative without an adversative particle.

Greek ἰδών ('having seen') and Latin videns render simple perception, whereas the Peshitta ܘܚܪ (root w-kh-r, 'gazed/looked intently') carries a more deliberate sense of fixed regard; the Syriac fuses the conjunction and verb into a single token corresponding to Greek καὶ ἰδών.

Greek τοὺς μαθητὰς αὐτοῦ and Latin discipulos suos express the possessive with a discrete pronoun, while the Peshitta encodes everything in the single inflected form ܒܬܠܡܝܕܘܗܝ with the prepositional ܒ ('upon') and the enclitic 3ms suffix, a typical Syriac synthetic construction.

Greek τῷ Πέτρῳ and Latin Petro give the Hellenised name 'Peter,' whereas the Peshitta reads ܒܫܡܥܘܢ ('Simon'), preserving the original Semitic name rather than the Greek translation of the Aramaic epithet Kephas; the Syriac also retains the preposition ܒ ('against') governing the object of rebuke.

Greek καὶ λέγει uses a coordinated finite present ('and he says'), the Vulgate subordinates with the participle dicens followed by a colon introducing direct speech, and the Peshitta employs the perfect ܘܐܡܪ ('and said')—an aspectual and syntactic difference in framing the quotation.

Greek ὕπαγε ('go away') and Latin Vade are single imperatives, but the Peshitta adds the ethic dative ܠܟ after ܙܠ (ܙܠ ܠܟ, 'go for yourself'), an idiomatic Semitic dativus ethicus with no equivalent in the Greek or Latin.

Greek ὀπίσω μου and Latin retro me express 'behind me' analytically with preposition plus pronoun, whereas the Peshitta condenses this into the single form ܠܒܣܬܪܝ ('to my rear') with the directional ܠ and 1cs suffix.
σατανᾶ / ܣܛܢܐ / Satana — vocative 'Satan,' a shared Semitic loanword.

Greek ὅτι οὐ ('because not') and Latin quoniam non keep the causal particle and negation separate, whereas the Peshitta fuses them into ܕܠܐ (relative/causal ܕ plus the negative ܠܐ), covering the function of both Greek words in a single token.

Greek φρονεῖς ('you set your mind on') and Latin sapis ('you savour/discern') render a single synthetic verb, whereas the Peshitta uses the participle ܪܢܐ ('you think/ponder') with the explicit enclitic pronoun ܐܢܬ as obligatory subject marker in the participial construction.

Greek τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ('the things of God') and Latin quæ Dei sunt use a substantivised article/relative with the genitive, while the Peshitta compresses to ܕܐܠܗܐ ('that of God') using the single relative-genitive particle ܕ; the verb sunt in Latin is supplied for the elliptical Greek.

Greek τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων and Latin quæ sunt hominum render 'the things of men' with article/relative plus genitive plural, whereas the Peshitta ܕܒܢܝ ܐܢܫܐ uses the idiomatic construct chain 'sons of men' (bnay nasha), a Semitic periphrasis for humankind absent from the Greek and Latin.
